units.intro: **Primary** characters = the gonads and genitalia you are born with. **Secondary** = puberty changes (voice, hair, breasts, hips) driven by sex hormones.

cards.title: 2.1 Primary and Secondary Sexual Characteristics
body: **Reproduction** is a biological process in which new individuals are produced from their parent(s).
Reproduction is important in ensuring the continuity of life and/or the species.
Reproduction also increases the number of individuals of a species.
In asexual reproduction only one parent produces offspring of the same genetic makeup.
Part or parts of an organism break off to produce more of the same kind, or the organism divides into two or more parts.

steps.text: **Step 1: Define primary sexual characteristics**
Primary sexual characteristics refer to the anatomical structures directly involved in reproduction that are present at birth.

Seminiferous tubules contain spermatogonia and Sertoli cells. The interstitial spaces between the tubules contain Leydig cells.

options.C: To provide motility for the sperm cell

cards.title: Puberty and sexual characters
body: **Primary sexual characters** are the reproductive organs present at birth (testes or ovaries). **Secondary sexual characters** develop at puberty under hormones: in boys (testosterone): deeper voice, facial and body hair, broader shoulders, bigger muscles; in girls (oestrogen): breasts develop, hips widen, menstruation begins, body hair grows.

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: Mucous - like fluid that lubricate the end of penis
options.B: Milky fluid that neutralizes the byproducts of the sperm

cards.why: The **seminal vesicles** produce about 60% of the volume of semen. This fluid is **alkaline** (to neutralize vaginal acidity) and contains fructose (energy for sperm) and **prostaglandins** (to stimulate contractions in the female reproductive tract).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: During oogenesis, the unequal division of cytoplasm results in the production of which of the following?

options.B: One diploid zygote and three polar bodies
options.C: One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body

cards.why:
**Step 1: Examine oogenesis division**
In meiosis I, the primary oocyte divides unequally.

**Step 2: Identify the products**
It yields one large haploid secondary oocyte (retaining most of the cytoplasm and nutrients) and one small, non-functional first polar body.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **One functional haploid secondary oocyte and a non-functional polar body**.

cards.title: 2.2 The male reproductive system — organ by organ
body: **What the system must do.** The male system has three jobs: (1) **make sperm cells** (male gametes), (2) **deliver them into the female tract**, and (3) **make the male sex hormone testosterone**.
**The nine organs to know** (textbook p.28): **testes, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, Cowper’s glands, scrotum, penis.** Group them so they are easy to remember:
**① Primary sex organs (gonads)** — the two **testes**: make sperm and testosterone.
**② Ducts (tubes)** — **epididymis → vas deferens → urethra**: store, mature and carry sperm.
**③ Accessory glands** — **seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper’s glands**: add the fluid part of semen.
**④ External organs** — **scrotum** (holds and cools the testes) and **penis** (places semen in the vagina).

**Primary vs secondary characters:** the genital organs above are **primary sexual characters** (present at birth). Changes at puberty — deep voice, beard, broad shoulders — are **secondary sexual characters** caused by testosterone.

cards.title: Follow one sperm: the route out of the body

steps.text: **Testis** — sperm are made in the seminiferous tubules.
**Epididymis** — hundreds of millions are stored and matured; they learn to swim.
**Vas deferens** (sperm duct) — muscular tube carries sperm up and round the bladder.
**Glands add fluid** — seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands; sperm + fluid = semen.
**Urethra** in the penis — semen leaves the body during ejaculation.

cards.title: The testes — where sperm and testosterone are made
body: **Shape and size:** two **oval (ovoid)** organs, about **5 cm long and 3 cm wide**. Each hangs from a **spermatic cord** (carrying blood vessels, nerves and the vas deferens) inside the sac-like **scrotum**.
**Why outside the body?** Body temperature (37 °C) is **too high** for normal sperm production. Sperm form best at **3–5 °C below** body temperature, so the testes hang outside the abdominal cavity.
**How they got there:** in the unborn baby the testes form inside the abdomen. **Testosterone**, secreted by the developing testes, makes them **descend into the scrotum**, usually before birth.

**Inside a testis:** it is packed with **highly coiled seminiferous tubules** (if stretched out, several hundred metres). The cells lining the inside of the tubules divide actively in mature males to make sperm (**spermatogenesis**).

**Between the tubules** are the **interstitial (Leydig) cells**, which secrete **testosterone** when stimulated by **LH**. Inside the tubules, nurse (**Sertoli**) cells feed the developing sperm (extra detail).
**So the testis is a mixed gland:** sperm leave through ducts (exocrine-like), testosterone goes into the blood (endocrine) — exactly what you met in 1.1.6.

cards.title: Spermatogenesis — how a sperm is made, step by step
body: **Step 1 — the stock.** Germ cells called **spermatogonia** are formed during **fetal life** and stored in the walls of the seminiferous tubules.
**Step 2 — the start.** At **puberty**, FSH (and testosterone) switch the tubules on. Spermatogonia divide by **mitosis** to keep up their numbers.

**Step 3 — halving the chromosomes.** Some cells grow into **primary spermatocytes** and divide by **meiosis**: 46 chromosomes → **23** in each **spermatid**. This is why a sperm carries only half the father’s genes.
**Step 4 — shaping.** Each round spermatid changes shape — grows a tail, packs its mitochondria, forms an acrosome — and becomes a **spermatozoon** (sperm).

**Step 5 — finishing school.** Sperm move to the **epididymis** to be stored and mature. The whole process takes about **two months**, and a healthy man makes **millions every day** from puberty to old age.
**Exam definition:** spermatogenesis is **the process of sperm cell formation** in the seminiferous tubules of the testes.

cards.title: Structure of the sperm cell — part by part

steps.text: **Head** — oval; holds a large **nucleus** with the father’s genetic material (23 chromosomes). Its front cap, the **acrosome**, contains **dissolving enzymes** to get through the coats of the ovum.
**Middle piece** — packed with **mitochondria**, which release energy (respiration) to drive the tail.
**Tail (flagellum)** — long and whip-like; lashes from side to side to **swim** through the uterus to the fallopian tube.
Sperm cells are among the **smallest** human cells, yet they must carry the father’s traits to the child.

cards.title: Male path
body: Testis (sperm + testosterone) → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra. Glands (seminal vesicles, prostate, Cowper’s) add fluid. Sperm need a bag 3–5 °C cooler than the body — that is why the testes hang outside.

cards.title: The ducts — epididymis, vas deferens, urethra
body: **Epididymis:** a long, tightly coiled tube formed by the **union of the seminiferous tubules**; it lies in close contact with the **outer surface of each testis**. Here **hundreds of millions of sperm are temporarily stored and matured**. The epididymis and tubules make secretions in which the sperm live and move.

**Vas deferens (sperm duct):** one from each epididymis. They run up into the body, loop over the bladder, **join together and open into the urethra**. Their muscular walls squeeze sperm along during ejaculation. (Cutting and tying them is **vasectomy**, a permanent family-planning method — semen still forms, but contains no sperm.)
**Urethra:** a **common tube** running through the centre of the penis. Both **urine and semen** pass through it — but **never at the same time**: during ejaculation a muscle closes the bladder neck.
**If sperm are not released** they break down and are **absorbed by the male’s body** (Exercise 2.2 Q1).

head: Gland
Secretion
Why it helps sperm
rows: Slightly **alkaline** fluid with **prostaglandins** (and fructose sugar — extra)
Regulates pH; prostaglandins make the female tract **contract**, helping sperm move towards the ovum; sugar = fuel
**Neutralises** the acidic sperm fluid (acid from wastes of stored sperm) and the acid of the vagina
**Lubricates** the end of the penis before intercourse

cards.title: Semen and ejaculation
body: **Semen** = sperm + secretions of the seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands. It is a **creamy-white suspension** that contains sperm **plus food and enzymes that make the sperm active**.

**Functions of the seminal fluid** (Exercise 2.2 Q3): (1) a **liquid medium** in which sperm swim; (2) **food** (sugar) for energy; (3) **alkali** to neutralise acids that would kill sperm; (4) **enzymes** that activate sperm; (5) **prostaglandins** that help sperm reach the ovum; (6) lubrication.
**Ejaculation:** a series of muscular **contractions** squeezes semen from the vas deferens and glands through the urethra and out of its **external opening**.

cards.title: Scrotum and penis — the external organs
body: **Scrotum:** a skin pouch that holds the **testes, the lower part of the spermatic cords and the epididymides**. It lies outside the body, behind the penis and in front of the upper thighs.

**The scrotum is a thermostat** (Do you know? p.31): normally its muscles are **relaxed** and the testes hang **away** from the warm body. If the temperature **drops too much**, the scrotal muscles **contract** and pull the testes **close to the body** to warm them. Even **tight underwear** that warms the testes can lower fertility.

**Penis:** made of **spongy (erectile) tissue and muscle**. During sexual arousal the spaces in the spongy tissue **fill with blood**, so the penis enlarges and hardens — an **erection** — and can enter the vagina to deposit semen.

**Foreskin and circumcision:** the tip of the penis is covered by a loose skin, the **foreskin**. Its surgical removal is **circumcision**. Hygiene point: an uncircumcised man must clean under the foreskin daily to avoid odour and bacterial infection.

cards.title: Step by step: the male reproductive system
body: **Step 1:** Testes (in the scrotum) produce sperm and the hormone testosterone; the scrotum keeps them about **3–5 °C below** body temperature, which sperm production needs.
**Step 2:** Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis.
**Step 3:** During ejaculation sperm travel through the vas deferens (sperm duct) to the urethra.

**Step 4:** Glands add seminal fluid: seminal vesicles (alkaline fluid, prostaglandins, sugar), prostate gland (thin milky alkaline fluid that neutralises acidity) and Cowper’s glands (lubricating mucus); sperm + fluid = semen.
**Step 5:** The urethra in the penis carries semen out of the body.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "SEVEN UP"
body: Seminiferous tubules, Epididymis, Vas deferens, Ejaculatory duct, (Nothing), Urethra, Penis.

cards.title: Memory hook — what the three glands add: “SPC”
body: Go down the urethra in order of the glands: **S**eminal vesicles → **P**rostate → **C**owper’s.

cards.title: Traps examiners love (2.2)
body: **Made vs stored:** sperm are **made** in the seminiferous tubules but **stored and matured** in the epididymis.
**Tubules vs Leydig cells:** tubules = sperm (FSH); Leydig (interstitial) cells = testosterone (LH).
**Vas deferens ≠ urethra:** the vas deferens carries only sperm; the urethra carries semen **or** urine.
**Which part enters the ovum?** The **head** (with its nucleus). The middle piece and tail are left outside.
**Prostate fluid is alkaline, not acidic** — it neutralises acid.
**Descent of the testes** is caused by **testosterone**, not by FSH.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: When asked for functions, give a reason too: e.g. "the scrotum is outside the body to keep the testes cooler, because sperm are made best below body temperature".

cards.title: Activity 2.2 Q1 — undescended testes
cards.problem: What happens if the testes fail to descend into the scrotum? Why?

steps.text: Step 1: Recall where sperm are made best — at 3–5 °C **below** body temperature.
Step 2: A testis that stays in the abdomen is kept at full body temperature (37 °C).
Step 3: At this temperature spermatogenesis fails, so few or no healthy sperm are made.
Step 4: If both testes stay inside, the man is **sterile (infertile)**, although testosterone may still be made, so he still develops male characters.
Step 5: The condition (cryptorchidism) is usually corrected by a small operation in early childhood.

cards.answer: The man becomes infertile because the higher body temperature stops sperm production; testosterone and male features may be normal.

cards.title: Activity 2.2 Q2 — adaptations of sperm
cards.problem: How are sperm cells adapted to perform their function?

steps.text: Step 1: Function = reach the ovum, enter it and deliver the father’s genes.
Step 2: Reach it → long **tail** for swimming; **mitochondria** in the middle piece supply energy.
Step 3: Enter it → **acrosome** enzymes dissolve the ovum’s outer coats.
Step 4: Deliver genes → head with a **haploid nucleus** (23 chromosomes); little cytoplasm so it is small and streamlined.
Step 5: Made in huge numbers → greater chance that one reaches the ovum.

cards.answer: Tail (swimming), mitochondria (energy), acrosome (enzymes to penetrate the ovum), haploid nucleus (genes), small streamlined shape and huge numbers.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q1
cards.problem: What will happen to mature sperm cells that are not released from the body?

steps.text: Step 1: Sperm are stored in the epididymis for a limited time.
Step 2: Old sperm that are not ejaculated break down.
Step 3: Their materials are reabsorbed by the body.

cards.answer: They break down and are absorbed by the male’s body.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q2
cards.problem: What is spermatogenesis?

steps.text: Step 1: “Sperm” + “genesis” (origin, making).
Step 2: Where — seminiferous tubules of the testes; when — from puberty.
Step 3: How — spermatogonia → mitosis → meiosis → spermatids → sperm.

cards.answer: Spermatogenesis is the formation of sperm cells from spermatogonia in the seminiferous tubules of the testes, beginning at puberty.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q3
cards.problem: What is the function of the seminal fluid?

steps.text: Step 1: Name the source — seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands.
Step 2: Medium — gives a liquid for sperm to swim in.
Step 3: Food and enzymes — sugar for energy, enzymes that activate sperm.
Step 4: Alkaline — neutralises acid in the male urethra and the vagina.
Step 5: Prostaglandins — cause contractions in the female tract that help sperm move to the ovum; mucus lubricates.

cards.answer: It carries the sperm, feeds and activates them, neutralises acids, helps their movement in the female tract and lubricates.

cards.title: Exercise 2.2 Q4
cards.problem: Which part of the sperm cell enters the ovum and is involved in fertilization?

steps.text: Step 1: The acrosome releases enzymes that open a path through the ovum’s coats.
Step 2: The **head** with its nucleus enters the ovum.
Step 3: The sperm nucleus fuses with the ovum nucleus → zygote.

cards.answer: The head (its nucleus fuses with the egg nucleus); the acrosome helps it get in.

cards.title: Let us discuss — is one parent’s gamete enough?
cards.problem: In sexual reproduction, is the gamete produced by one parent enough to produce a zygote? Why?

steps.text: Step 1: Gametes are made by meiosis, so each has only **half** the chromosomes (23 in humans).
Step 2: A zygote must have the full **46**.
Step 3: So a sperm (23) must fuse with an ovum (23) → 46.

cards.answer: No. Each gamete is haploid (23 chromosomes); fusion of a male and a female gamete restores the diploid number (46) in the zygote.

cards.title: Apply it — vasectomy
cards.problem: A man has both vasa deferentia cut and tied. Explain whether he still (a) ejaculates, (b) is fertile, (c) has a deep voice.

steps.text: Step 1: (a) The glands are untouched, so he still ejaculates semen — but it contains **no sperm**.
Step 2: (b) With no sperm in the semen he is **infertile** (vasectomy is a permanent contraceptive).
Step 3: (c) Testosterone goes into the **blood**, not through the vas deferens, so male characters stay normal.

cards.answer: (a) Yes, semen without sperm; (b) no, he is sterile; (c) yes, testosterone still reaches the blood.

cards.title: 2.3 The female reproductive system — what it must do
body: **Five jobs:** make **ova** (eggs) and female sex hormones; receive sperm (**conception**); hold and feed the **developing fetus**; give **birth**; and **feed the baby** with milk.
**Internal (major) organs:** **ovaries, fallopian tubes (oviducts), uterus, vagina** — all inside the pelvis.
**External (accessory) organs:** the **vulva** and the **mammary glands** (breasts).
**Compare with the male:** ovary ↔ testis (gonad); oviduct ↔ sperm duct (tube); but the female has a uterus to carry the baby, so her system has **more jobs** than the male’s.

cards.title: The female organs — from ovary to the outside

steps.text: **Ovaries** — two oval glands; make ova and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone.
**Fallopian tubes** — funnel with fimbriae catches the ovum; cilia move it; **fertilization happens here** (upper part).
**Uterus (womb)** — muscular, pear-shaped; the embryo implants in its lining (endometrium).
**Cervix** — the muscular neck of the uterus that projects into the vagina.
**Vagina** — 10–15 cm tube; receives the penis and sperm; the birth canal.

cards.title: Ovaries — the female gonads
body: **Position:** two **oval** organs in the pelvis, **one on each side of the uterus**, attached to the body wall and anchored to the uterus by the **ovarian ligament**.
**When they start:** at **puberty** the **pituitary** (FSH and LH) stimulates them to become functional.
**Job 1 — ova.** Each ovum develops inside a fluid-filled **follicle**. About once a month one follicle bursts and releases its ovum — **ovulation**.

**Job 2 — hormones.** The **follicle** makes **oestrogen** (female characters, rebuilds the uterine lining). After ovulation the empty follicle turns into the **corpus luteum** (“yellow body”), which makes **progesterone** to prepare and keep the uterus ready for a fertilized ovum.
**So the ovary, like the testis, is a mixed gland:** gametes out, hormones into the blood.

cards.title: Oogenesis — the numbers behind the eggs
body: **Step 1 — at birth:** a girl’s ovaries already hold about **two million** potential ova. No new ones are made after birth (very different from sperm).
**Step 2 — before puberty:** about **75 %** degenerate, leaving a few **hundred thousand**.
**Step 3 — puberty to menopause:** each month **one** ovary releases **one** ovum ready for fertilization. Over a lifetime only **400–500** become mature ova.

**Step 4 — the meiosis twist (extra):** egg cells start meiosis before birth and pause; the ovum completes meiosis only if a sperm enters. Each division gives **one large ovum** (with nearly all the cytoplasm) and tiny **polar bodies** that die.
**Definitions:** **oogenesis** = production of ova in the ovaries; **ovulation** = release of a mature ovum from the ovary; **menopause** = the end of menstrual cycles.

cards.title: Structure of the ovum
body: **Nucleus** — the mother’s 23 chromosomes. **Cytoplasm with yolk** — food for the first days after fertilization. **Jelly coat** and **follicle cells** — protective layers the sperm’s acrosome enzymes must dissolve. **No tail** — the ovum is moved by cilia and muscle in the oviduct.

cards.title: Fallopian tubes (oviducts) — the meeting place
body: **Structure:** two tubes, one each side of the uterus. Each starts as a **funnel** with finger-like **fimbriae** lying close to (but **not joined to**) the ovary, runs downward and inward, and joins the top of the uterus.
**Catching the ovum:** at ovulation the fimbriae sweep over the ovary and the ovum is drawn into the funnel.
**Moving the ovum:** the ovum cannot swim. **Cilia** lining the tube beat towards the uterus and the muscular wall contracts gently (peristalsis).
**Fertilization site:** sperm swim up to meet the ovum in the **upper region of the fallopian tube**. The zygote then takes several days to reach the uterus.
**Why a blocked tube matters:** if the tubes are blocked (e.g. by infection) sperm and ovum cannot meet → infertility; tying the tubes (tubal ligation) is a permanent contraceptive.

cards.title: The uterus (womb) and cervix — the life-support system
body: **Shape and size:** a hollow, muscular, **pear-shaped** organ (the textbook prints “pearl-shaped” — it means pear), about the size of a **fist** when not pregnant. It lies **behind the bladder** (and in front of the rectum).

**Three layers (extra detail):** outer covering; thick **muscle (myometrium)** that contracts strongly in labour; inner lining (**endometrium**) rich in blood vessels and glands — thickens every month and is shed at menstruation.
**Function:** the place where the fertilized egg **implants, receives nourishment and develops into a fetus**. It stretches enormously during pregnancy and pushes the baby out at birth.
**Cervix:** the lower, muscular **neck** of the uterus that projects into the vagina. It stays tightly closed during pregnancy and **dilates (widens)** during childbirth.

cards.title: Vagina, vulva and mammary glands
body: **Vagina:** a muscular tube **10–15 cm** long connecting the uterus (cervix) to the outside. It **receives the penis and sperm**, lets the menstrual flow out, and is the **birth canal**. It is **separate from the urethra** (unlike the male, the female has separate openings for urine and reproduction).

**Hymen:** a thin mucous membrane partly covering the vaginal opening. It usually has **one or more holes**, which let menstrual blood out; the openings are usually enlarged at first intercourse — but the hymen can also stretch or tear in **sport, heavy exercise or accidents**, so its state is **not** proof of virginity.

**Vulva:** the **external genitalia** — the **vestibule** (space into which the vagina and urethra open) with its surrounding structures: outer lips (**labia majora**), inner lips (**labia minora**) and, in front, the small sensitive **clitoris** with erectile tissue.
**Mammary glands:** organs of **milk production** inside the breasts. They enlarge at puberty under **oestrogen and progesterone**; after birth **prolactin** makes milk and **oxytocin** ejects it.

cards.title: Exercise 2.3 Q1 / Activity 2.4 — the hymen
cards.problem: What is the hymen? How does the menstrual flow leave the uterus when the hymen is present? Does the absence of an intact hymen show that a woman has had intercourse?

steps.text: Step 1: Definition — a thin mucous membrane that partly covers the vaginal opening.
Step 2: It normally has **one or more openings**, so menstrual blood flows out through them.
Step 3: The hymen can stretch or tear during heavy exercise, sport, cycling, horse-riding or accidents; some girls are born with very little hymen.
Step 4: So an absent or torn hymen is **not proof** of intercourse.

cards.answer: A thin membrane over the vaginal opening with small holes through which the menstrual flow passes; it can be broken without intercourse, so its absence is not proof of sexual activity.

steps.text: Step 2: Fraction maturing = 450 ÷ 500 000 = 0.0009.

cards.title: Activity 2.5
cards.problem: (1) What is the role of the ovum in reproduction? (2) What is the function of the uterus?

steps.text: Step 1: The ovum is the female gamete — it carries the mother’s 23 chromosomes and food (yolk).
Step 2: When fertilized it forms the zygote, which grows into the new individual.
Step 3: The uterus receives the embryo, lets it implant, nourishes it through the placenta, protects it, and pushes it out at birth.

cards.answer: (1) Supplies the mother’s genes and the first food for the zygote. (2) Implantation, nourishment, protection and growth of the fetus; contractions at birth.

cards.title: Cycle — 28-day story
body: FSH grows a follicle; oestrogen rebuilds the uterus lining; LH surge ~day 14 ovulates; corpus luteum makes progesterone to keep the lining; if no embryo, progesterone falls and the lining is shed (menstruation).

cards.title: Mnemonic — FOLP
body: FSH → Oestrogen → LH → Progesterone. “First Open the Lining, then Protect it.”

cards.title: Fertilisation to contraception — 30-second story
body: **Fertilisation** in the oviduct. Zygote → blastocyst implants. Placenta feeds and exchanges gases; amniotic sac cushions. Birth: oxytocin (posterior pituitary) helps contractions.
**Contraception** methods: barrier, hormonal (stop ovulation), IUD, natural / calendar (least reliable), sterilisation. Exam: name the method and the *how* (block sperm / stop egg / stop implant).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Menstruation and the menstrual cycle
body: **Step 1 — preparing a bed.** After ovulation the **corpus luteum** produces **progesterone**, which makes the uterine wall (endometrium) **thick, soft and rich in blood vessels**, ready to receive a fertilized ovum.
**Step 2 — no baby, no bed.** If the ovum is **not fertilized** or **implantation fails**, the corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls, and the thick wall **breaks down**.
**Step 3 — the flow.** The endometrial lining and the unfertilized ovum are discharged **with blood** through the vagina. This periodic flow of blood and tissue is **menstruation** (a “period”).
**Step 4 — rebuild.** After menstruation, oestrogen from a new growing follicle makes the lining **build up again**.
**The menstrual cycle** = this repeated building up and shedding of the lining plus the release of an ovum, about **every 28 days**, from **puberty** to **menopause**.

cards.title: The three phases on a 28-day timeline

steps.text: **Menstrual phase (days 1–5, 4–5 days):** blood, vessels and endometrial tissue are shed.
**Proliferative / follicular phase (days 5–14, 9–10 days):** the lining **proliferates** (grows rapidly) while ovarian follicles develop and make oestrogen.
**Ovulation (about day 14):** an LH surge makes the ripe follicle burst and release the ovum. The day varies between women and between cycles.
**Secretory / luteal phase (days 14–28, 12–14 days):** uterine glands mature and **secrete**; the **corpus luteum** (luteal) makes progesterone.

cards.title: Why the names make sense
body: **Proliferative** = proliferation (fast growth) of the uterine mucosa. **Follicular** = the ovarian follicles develop.
**Secretory** = uterine glands secrete. **Luteal** = the corpus **luteum** is present.
**Rule:** the uterus name and the ovary name describe the **same days** from two organs.

cards.title: Menopause — when the cycles stop
body: **When:** at about **40–50 years**, cycles become **irregular**, ovulation stops, and finally cycles stop completely — **menopause**.
**Why:** age-related changes in the ovaries — **very few follicles remain**, and those that remain are **less sensitive to FSH and LH**, however high these hormones are.
**Result:** oestrogen and progesterone fall, so FSH and LH actually **rise** (no negative feedback).
**Males (Activity 2.7 Q3):** men have **no true menopause** — sperm and testosterone production fall only slowly with age.

cards.title: Calculate — ovulation and the fertile days
cards.problem: Ruth’s period started on 3 March and her cycles are a regular 28 days. (a) On what date does she probably ovulate? (b) Ovulation happens about 14 days before the NEXT period. If Selam has a regular 32-day cycle, on which cycle day does she ovulate?

steps.text: Step 1: Day 1 = 3 March, so day 14 = 3 + 13 = **16 March**.
Step 2: For a 32-day cycle, the luteal phase is still about 14 days.
Step 3: Ovulation day = 32 − 14 = **day 18**.
Step 4: Fertile window: sperm live a few days and the ovum ≈ 24 h, so the days just before and on ovulation are most fertile — this is why “safe-period” counting is unreliable when cycles vary.

cards.title: Explain — why menstruation stops in pregnancy
cards.problem: Why does a pregnant woman not menstruate?

steps.text: Step 1: Menstruation happens when progesterone falls.
Step 2: In pregnancy the corpus luteum, and later the **placenta**, keep secreting progesterone (and oestrogen).
Step 3: High progesterone keeps the lining in place and stops new follicles developing, so no ovulation or menstruation.

cards.answer: Progesterone stays high (corpus luteum, then placenta), so the lining is not shed and ovulation is prevented.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The secretory phase is also called the luteal phase because
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Luteal comes from corpus luteum.

**Step 2:** It is present from ovulation to the end of the cycle.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: 2.3.2 Hormonal control of reproduction — the chain of command
body: **Step 1 — brain.** The **hypothalamus** produces **gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)**, which travels to the anterior pituitary.
**Step 2 — pituitary.** GnRH makes the pituitary secrete **FSH** and **LH**.

**Step 3 — puberty switch.** Before puberty a small amount of testosterone and other **androgens** **inhibit** GnRH release. At puberty the hypothalamus becomes **less sensitive** to this inhibition, GnRH rises, and so do LH and FSH.
**Step 4 — FSH** stimulates the **seminiferous tubules** (sperm formation) in males and the **growth of follicles** in females; the cells round a developing ovum make **oestrogen**.
**Step 5 — LH** makes the **interstitial cells** of the testes secrete more **testosterone**; in females it causes ovulation and makes the **corpus luteum** produce **progesterone**.

**Step 6 — the outcome.** If the egg is fertilized, progesterone **keeps the uterine lining** from breaking down. If not, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone stops, and **menstruation** follows.

cards.title: Feedback — how the hormones talk to each other
body: **Negative feedback (most of the cycle):** rising oestrogen and progesterone (or testosterone in males) **reduce** GnRH, FSH and LH. This keeps only **one** follicle developing at a time and keeps male hormone levels steady.
**Positive feedback (just before ovulation):** when oestrogen from the ripe follicle reaches a **high peak**, it does the opposite and triggers a **surge of LH** → ovulation.
**After ovulation:** high progesterone holds FSH and LH down, so no new follicle grows; when the corpus luteum dies, the brake is released and FSH rises again → a new cycle.
**Application:** the contraceptive pill supplies oestrogen/progesterone, keeping FSH and LH low, so no follicle matures and no ovulation occurs.

cards.title: Memory hook — order of hormones in a cycle: FOLP
body: “**F**irst **O**pen the **L**ining, then **P**rotect it.”

cards.title: Activity 2.6 Q1
cards.problem: What is the function of the testosterone found in males before puberty?

steps.text: Step 1: Before birth, testosterone from the developing testes makes them **descend into the scrotum** and the male organs form.
Step 2: In childhood the small amount present **inhibits GnRH**, so FSH and LH stay low.
Step 3: This keeps puberty from starting too early.

cards.answer: It causes descent of the testes (before birth) and, in childhood, inhibits GnRH release so that puberty does not start early.

cards.title: Activity 2.6 Q2
cards.problem: Can fertilization take place in the uterus? Why?

steps.text: Step 1: The ovum lives only about **24 hours** after ovulation.
Step 2: It moves slowly down the tube and needs several days to reach the uterus.
Step 3: So by the time it reaches the uterus it has degenerated; normally fertilization occurs in the **upper fallopian tube**.

cards.answer: Normally no — the ovum dies within about 24 hours, long before it reaches the uterus, so fertilization happens in the upper oviduct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: At puberty GnRH secretion increases because the hypothalamus

options.B: becomes less sensitive to the inhibitory effect of androgens

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Before puberty androgens hold GnRH back.

**Step 2:** At puberty the hypothalamus becomes less sensitive to that brake → more GnRH.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: 2.3.3 Fertilization and pregnancy — the journey step by step
body: **Step 1 — ovulation.** Roughly every **28 days** one ovum is released, usually **alternately** from the two ovaries. Cilia move it down the fallopian tube. It lives only about **24 hours**.

**Step 2 — sperm arrive.** During intercourse (copulation) millions of sperm are released into the vagina. They swim through the cervix and uterus into the fallopian tube. (The textbook gives 3–5 million per cm³ of semen; medical references give tens of millions per cm³ — remember simply “millions”.) Sperm can live in the female tract for **a few days**.

**Step 3 — fertilization.** Several sperm reach the ovum, but **only one** enters. Its nucleus **fuses** with the ovum nucleus → **zygote** (46 chromosomes). This happens in the **upper region of the fallopian tube**.
**Step 4 — cleavage.** The zygote divides by **mitosis** — 2, 4, 8, 16 cells… — forming a ball of cells while moving down the tube. Pregnancy has begun.
**Step 5 — implantation.** The ball of cells reaches the uterus and the embryo **implants** in the thickened wall, obtaining food from it.
**Step 6 — keeping the pregnancy.** Progesterone (corpus luteum) maintains the uterus and stops follicles developing → no ovulation, no menstruation.

cards.title: Placenta, membranes and umbilical cord
body: **Placenta:** a special tissue made by the growing embryo and firmly joined to the uterine wall. It **absorbs nutrients and oxygen** from the mother and passes **wastes (CO₂, urea)** back. As it grows it secretes **oestrogen and progesterone**; then the corpus luteum degenerates and the placenta keeps the embryo attached.
**Chorion:** the outer membrane that protects the embryo (and forms part of the placenta).
**Amnion:** a sac containing **amniotic fluid** — a watery environment and a **shock absorber**.

**Umbilical cord:** a long cord joining the embryo to the placenta. The **umbilical vein** carries **food and oxygenated blood** to the embryo; the **umbilical arteries** carry **wastes and deoxygenated blood** back to the placenta. (Vessels are named by direction — veins go **towards** the heart, arteries **away** — not by how much oxygen they carry.)

**No direct mixing:** mother’s and baby’s blood do **not** mix; materials diffuse across the thin barrier **in the placenta** (the textbook says “through the umbilical cord” — the cord only carries the baby’s blood to and from the placenta).
**Gestation:** pregnancy usually lasts **38–40 weeks** (about 9 months).

cards.title: Exercise 2.3 Q3 — twins
cards.problem: What are the differences between fraternal, identical and Siamese twins?

steps.text: Step 1: Count the eggs and sperm — fraternal: **2 ova + 2 sperm**; identical and Siamese: **1 ovum + 1 sperm**.
Step 2: Genes — fraternal twins differ (may be boy and girl); identical/Siamese have the same genes and sex.
Step 3: Separation — identical twins separate fully; Siamese twins do not and are born joined.

cards.answer: Fraternal: two eggs fertilized by two sperm — genetically different. Identical: one zygote splits into two — genetically identical. Siamese: one zygote splits incompletely — identical twins born joined.

cards.title: Number work — cleavage
cards.problem: A zygote divides by mitosis every 12 hours. How many cells are there after 2 days (assume all divisions are regular)?

steps.text: Step 1: 2 days = 48 hours = 48 ÷ 12 = 4 divisions.
Step 2: Cells double each time: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16.
Step 3: Formula: 2ⁿ = 2⁴ = 16.

cards.title: Why only a short fertile period?
cards.problem: Sperm can live a few days in the female tract. Why is the period in which fertilization can occur still short?

steps.text: Step 1: The limiting cell is the ovum.
Step 2: The ovum degenerates about 24 hours after ovulation.
Step 3: So fertilization is possible only if sperm are present in the tube in the days just before or within a day after ovulation.

cards.answer: Because the ovum survives only about 24 hours after ovulation.

options.B: oxygenated blood and food to the embryo

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Vein = towards the baby’s heart.

**Step 2:** It carries food and oxygen from the placenta.

cards.problem: Usual site in humans?

steps.text: Oviduct / fallopian tube.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Childbirth (parturition) — step by step
body: **Step 1 — labour begins.** Towards the end of gestation the thick muscular wall of the uterus starts **regular, powerful contractions** (labour). **Oxytocin** from the posterior pituitary strengthens them by **positive feedback** (link to 1.1.1).
**Step 2 — the waters break.** The abdominal wall contracts too; the **amnion bursts** and amniotic fluid flows out through the vagina, **lubricating the birth canal**.
**Step 3 — opening.** The **cervix and vagina dilate** (widen).
**Step 4 — birth.** The fetus, usually **head first** towards the cervix, gradually emerges through the vagina — **birth or parturition**.
**Step 5 — afterbirth.** The cord is clamped and cut. Further contractions push out the **placenta** and the remaining part of the umbilical cord — together called the **afterbirth**.
**Step 6 — the navel.** The stump of cord on the baby dries and falls off, leaving a scar — the **navel**.
**Step 7 — care.** By instinct the baby suckles; **prolactin** makes milk and **oxytocin** lets it flow. Breast milk gives nutrients and antibodies. Humans care for their young for many years.

cards.title: Exercise 2.3 Q2 — afterbirth
cards.problem: What is afterbirth?

steps.text: Step 1: After the baby is born the uterus keeps contracting.
Step 2: These contractions expel the placenta and the part of the umbilical cord left inside.

cards.answer: The placenta and the remaining umbilical cord, pushed out by contractions of the uterus and abdominal wall after the baby is born.

cards.title: Activity 2.7 Q1
cards.problem: Is it possible to know the sex of an unborn baby? How?

steps.text: Step 1: Yes — sex is fixed at fertilization (XX girl, XY boy).
Step 2: An **ultrasound** scan (from about 18–20 weeks) shows the external genitals.
Step 3: Tests of fetal cells (amniocentesis) can show the chromosomes, but are used only for medical reasons.

cards.answer: Yes, mainly by ultrasound scanning; chromosome tests of fetal cells can also show it.

cards.q: Which hormone increases uterine contractions during labour?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Contractions of the uterus = oxytocin.

**Step 2:** Prolactin is for milk production; progesterone actually relaxes the uterus.

**Answer: B.**

cards.title: Traps examiners love (2.3)
body: **Fertilization** happens in the **oviduct**; **implantation** in the **uterus**.
**Follicle → oestrogen; corpus luteum → progesterone.** Do not swap them.
**The ovum has no tail**; it is moved by cilia.
**Umbilical vein = oxygenated** (to the baby).
**Fraternal = 2 eggs; identical = 1 egg.**
**Menstruation** = shedding of the lining because progesterone falls — not because oestrogen rises.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the structural and functional relationship between the ovaries and the fallopian tubes?

options.A: The ovaries are physically fused to the fallopian tubes to prevent egg loss.
options.B: The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.
options.C: Ovaries develop inside the fallopian tubes during fetal life.
options.D: The fallopian tubes secrete estrogen to stimulate ovarian follicle development.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze female reproductive anatomy**
The ovaries and fallopian tubes are not physically continuous. The opening of the fallopian tube lies close to the ovary.

**Step 2: Understand egg capture**
The funnel-shaped end of the fallopian tube has finger-like projections (fimbriae) that capture the released oocyte and draw it into the tube.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct choice is **The fallopian tubes are separate but have finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovulated egg from the ovary.**

**Step 2:** Sperm swim up through the uterus into the oviduct, where they meet the egg.

cards.title: 2.4 Contraception
body: Contraception can be defined as any means used to prevent a pregnancy.
Birth control includes the use of devices, drugs or surgery.
A family may be forced to determine the number of children it would like to have for reasons such as finance, the mother’s health, etc.
Contraception is used to avoid unwanted pregnancies in young girls who are not ready to take care of children.

cards.title: Step by step: Contraception
body: **Step 1:** Contraception means methods used to prevent pregnancy by stopping sperm from meeting the egg or stopping implantation.
**Step 2:** Natural methods: abstinence (100 % effective) and the rhythm/calendar method (avoiding intercourse around ovulation – unreliable).
**Step 3:** Barrier methods: male and female condoms and the diaphragm stop sperm reaching the egg; condoms also protect against STIs including HIV.
**Step 4:** Hormonal methods: the pill, injections and implants contain hormones that stop ovulation; the IUD prevents implantation.
**Step 5:** Surgical (permanent) methods: vasectomy (cutting the sperm ducts) and tubal ligation (cutting/tying the oviducts).

**Example:** A couple wants to delay children and also avoid any risk of infection: the condom is the best single choice because it is a barrier to sperm and to infections; the pill alone would not protect against STIs.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "No sex, Natural, Barrier, Hormone, Surgery"

cards.title: Exam tip

**Step 3: Final Result**

**Step 1:** Most methods only prevent pregnancy.

questions.q: A health educator at the hospital in Keren traces the route followed by sperm from the site of their formation to the point where they leave the male body through the urethra. According to the unit's SEVEN UP pathway, how many structures does a spermatozoon pass through during this journey, and what are they in order?

options.A: 4 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, urethra
options.B: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, vas deferens, epididymis, ejaculatory duct, penis
options.C: 5 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, urethra, penis
options.D: 6 structures: seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis

why: **Recall the SEVEN UP acronym.** The memory aid SEVEN UP gives the path of sperm: S = Seminiferous tubules, E = Epididymis, V = Vas deferens, E = Ejaculatory duct, N = Nothing (a placeholder, not a structure), U = Urethra, P = Penis. Only the six lettered structures carry sperm; the N entry is a memory aid with no anatomical counterpart.

**Check each structure against its stated role.** Seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis; the epididymis stores spermatozoa and allows them to acquire motility; the vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum and loops over the urinary bladder; the ejaculatory duct is where the vas deferens joins; the urethra is the final tube; and the penis delivers semen.

**Reject the distractor pathways.** Options A and B place the vas deferens before the epididymis, but sperm enter the epididymis directly from the tubules and only later are propelled into the vas deferens. Options B and C omit the ejaculatory duct, which the unit explicitly lists between the vas deferens and the urethra. Options A and C also stop at the urethra and drop the penis.
**Count and conclude.** Six lettered structures remain once the placeholder N is excluded, giving the order seminiferous tubules, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra, penis.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that contradict the unit notes, then choose the one that matches every detail in the question.

**Move to the next structure.** During sexual arousal, mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens, the thick-walled muscular duct that exits the scrotum, traverses the inguinal canal into the abdominal cavity, and loops over the urinary bladder.
**Identify the end point.** The vas deferens loops over the urinary bladder to join the ejaculatory duct, which is the stated end of this stretch.
**Count and conclude.** Labelling the epididymis, the vas deferens and the ejaculatory duct gives three structures in that order.

questions.q: A clinical technician in Asmara records a man's core body temperature as $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The unit states that spermatogenesis cannot occur effectively at core body temperature, and that the scrotum maintains an optimal microenvironment approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core body temperature. Calculate the full optimal scrotal temperature range, then state which of the following scrotal measurements would fall inside that range: $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ or $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
questions.answer: Optimal scrotal range = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$; the only measurement inside this range is $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$.
why: **State the governing principle.** The scrotum holds the testes outside the pelvic cavity so that sperm production occurs several degrees below core temperature, because high temperatures degrade the key germinal enzymes needed for spermatogenesis. The permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.
**Compute the upper end of the range.** The upper end is only $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compute the lower end of the range.** The lower end is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. The optimal range is therefore $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ inclusive.

**Test each candidate measurement.** Compare each value with the interval $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C} \leq T \leq 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. For $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference from core is $$4.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which lies between $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ and $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it is inside. For $$34.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ the difference is only $$2.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; for $$35.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$1.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$; and for $$36.2^{\circ}\text{C}$$ it is $$0.8^{\circ}\text{C}$$. All three are less than $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature and therefore lie above $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, outside the range.
**Conclude.** The optimal scrotal temperature range is $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and of the four measurements only $$32.5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ falls within it.

questions.q: At a clinic in Massawa the ambient heat is high, and a technician notes that a man's testes are held at the extreme cool end of the permitted range while his core temperature reads $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. If the permitted differential is $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, calculate the temperature of the testes and state how many degrees cooler than core temperature this is.
questions.answer: Testicular temperature = $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, which is $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature
why: **Identify the relevant end of the range.** The extreme cool end corresponds to the largest permitted differential, which the unit gives as $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core body temperature. Under warm conditions the dartos and cremaster muscles relax to promote heat loss, which drives the testes toward this cool end.

**Substitute the core temperature.** Using core body temperature $$= 37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, the extreme cool testicular temperature is $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Check against the full range.** The full range spans $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 5^{\circ}\text{C} = 32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 3^{\circ}\text{C} = 34.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$, and $$32.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is indeed the lowest value in that interval.

**State the cooling differential.** Subtracting the testicular temperature from the core temperature gives $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 32.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 5^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so the testes are held $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature.

questions.q: A man in Asmara takes a prolonged hot bath and his scrotal temperature rises to $$36.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ while his core temperature remains $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$. Calculate how far this scrotal temperature lies below core temperature, and state whether it satisfies the $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential required for effective spermatogenesis.
questions.answer: Only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, so it does not satisfy the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential and spermatogenesis is impaired
why: **Calculate the actual differential.** The differential is core temperature minus scrotal temperature: $$37.0^{\circ}\text{C} - 36.0^{\circ}\text{C} = 1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$.

**Compare with the required differential.** Effective spermatogenesis requires the testes to be approximately $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ cooler than core temperature. The measured differential of $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ is smaller than the minimum of $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$, so it falls short of the requirement.

**Relate the shortfall to enzyme function.** Spermatogenesis cannot proceed effectively at temperatures close to core body temperature because heat degrades key germinal enzymes. A differential of only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ leaves the testes far too warm for normal germ-cell development.

**Conclude.** The hot bath leaves the testes only $$1.0^{\circ}\text{C}$$ below core temperature, which fails the required $$3^{\circ}\text{C}$$ to $$5^{\circ}\text{C}$$ differential, so sperm production is impaired.

questions.q: At a reproductive health session in Keren, a facilitator explains that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of the total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$, with the remainder coming from the bulbourethral glands and the spermatozoa themselves. If a single ejaculation has a total volume of $$3.0\text{ mL}$$, calculate the volume contributed by the seminal vesicles, the volume contributed by the prostate gland, and the combined volume contributed by all remaining sources.
questions.answer: Seminal vesicles $$= 1.8\text{ mL}$$; prostate gland $$= 0.9\text{ mL}$$; all remaining sources $$= 0.3\text{ mL}$$ (together these sum to the $$3.0\text{ mL}$$ total).
why: **Identify the known quantities.** Total semen volume $$= 3.0\text{ mL}$$. Seminal vesicle contribution $$= 60\%$$ of total. Prostate gland contribution $$= 30\%$$ of total. The bulbourethral glands and spermatozoa account for whatever remains.

**Calculate the seminal vesicle volume.** Multiply the total volume by the seminal vesicle fraction: $$0.60 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 1.8\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fluid supplies fructose as metabolic fuel for sperm and prostaglandins that trigger contractions in the female reproductive tract, which is consistent with this gland providing the bulk of semen volume.

**Calculate the prostate gland volume.** Multiply the total volume by the prostate fraction: $$0.30 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.9\text{ mL}$$. This thin, milky, slightly alkaline fluid contains citric acid and proteolytic enzymes that liquefy the semen coagulum after ejaculation.

**Calculate the remaining volume.** First find the remaining percentage: $$100\% - 60\% - 30\% = 10\%$$. Then apply it: $$0.10 \times 3.0\text{ mL} = 0.3\text{ mL}$$. This residue corresponds to the clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus of the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands together with the spermatozoa.
**Check the total.** Add the parts: $$1.8\text{ mL} + 0.9\text{ mL} + 0.3\text{ mL} = 3.0\text{ mL}$$, which matches the stated total volume, so the calculation is consistent.

questions.q: A laboratory in Asmara receives a semen sample of $$2.5\text{ mL}$$ for analysis. Using the unit's values of $$60\%$$ for the seminal vesicles, $$30\%$$ for the prostate gland and the remaining percentage for the bulbourethral glands plus spermatozoa, calculate the volume contributed by each of the three components.

why: **Set out the sample volume and fractions.** Total volume $$= 2.5\text{ mL}$$, seminal vesicle fraction $$= 0.60$$, prostate fraction $$= 0.30$$, and the remaining fraction is $$1 - 0.60 - 0.30 = 0.10$$.
**Compute the seminal vesicle share.** $$0.60 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 1.5\text{ mL}$$. This alkaline fructose- and prostaglandin-rich fluid is the largest single contributor to semen volume.

**Compute the remaining share.** $$0.10 \times 2.5\text{ mL} = 0.25\text{ mL}$$, representing the clear lubricating mucus of the bulbourethral glands plus the spermatozoa.
**Verify the total.** $$1.5\text{ mL} + 0.75\text{ mL} + 0.25\text{ mL} = 2.5\text{ mL}$$, matching the sample volume.

questions.q: A man in Massawa has been unable to conceive with his partner for two years. Semen analysis shows that sperm are being produced in normal numbers but almost all of them are immotile and none has acquired fertilizing capability, while the man's reproductive hormone levels are normal. Using only the structures and functions described in this unit, identify the single structure whose function is most likely impaired, and justify your answer with two functions of that structure.
questions.answer: The epididymis. It normally stores spermatozoa and provides the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability; normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm point to failure of exactly these two functions.
why: **Note that sperm production itself is intact.** The seminiferous tubules are the site of spermatogenesis and the Sertoli cells provide nutrients and structural support to developing germ cells. Because sperm are produced in normal numbers, this function is clearly not the problem. The acrosome, which carries the hydrolytic enzymes needed to digest the egg's protective layers, is also formed during spermiogenesis in the testis, so the production line is working.

**Identify which function is missing.** The two missing features are motility and fertilizing capability. The unit states that sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability during their residence in the epididymis, where they undergo biochemical maturation over several weeks.

**Match the missing functions to the correct structure.** The epididymis is the crescent-shaped tubule coiled on the superior-posterior margin of each testis in which spermatozoa reside for several weeks. Its two functions are (i) storing spermatozoa and (ii) facilitating the biochemical maturation by which sperm acquire independent motility and fertilizing capability. An impairment of this structure explains normal sperm numbers with immotile, non-fertilizing sperm.

**Confirm that the other ducts are not implicated.** The vas deferens is a thick-walled muscular duct that simply transports mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct; it does not mature sperm. The unit also notes that mature sperm are propelled from the tail of the epididymis into the vas deferens only during sexual arousal, whereas the immotility described here is a property of the sperm themselves, present regardless of arousal.

**Conclude.** The impaired structure is the epididymis, because the sperm have normal production but lack precisely the two properties, motility and fertilizing capability, that the epididymis confers during maturation.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man in Asmara undergoes a vasectomy in which the vas deferens is cut and sealed. His testes continue to produce sperm and his Leydig cells continue to secrete testosterone. Explain, using only the unit's description of the male tract and of semen composition, what happens to the sperm produced after the operation and why the operation does not reduce his testosterone levels.
questions.answer: Sperm are still produced in the seminiferous tubules and mature in the epididymis, but they can no longer pass beyond the sealed vas deferens, so they are not included in the ejaculate; testosterone is unaffected because it is secreted by the Leydig cells, which the unit places under the control of LH from the anterior pituitary, not under the control of the vas deferens.
why: **Locate the cut in the pathway.** The vas deferens is the thick-walled muscular duct that carries mature sperm from the tail of the epididymis out of the scrotum, through the inguinal canal and over the urinary bladder to the ejaculatory duct. Sealing it blocks this single transport route.

**Trace the fate of the sperm.** Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules is unaffected, and sperm still pass into the epididymis to mature. However, they cannot be propelled beyond the blocked vas deferens, so no sperm reach the ejaculatory duct and urethra and none appear in the ejaculate, which is why vasectomy is a permanent surgical contraceptive method.

**Locate the source of testosterone.** In the interstitial space between adjacent seminiferous tubules lie the Leydig cells, which synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone from the anterior pituitary. These cells are entirely separate from the vas deferens.

**Explain why testosterone is unchanged.** Because the Leydig cells and the HPG axis that regulates them are untouched by the operation, testosterone secretion continues normally. Only the sperm delivery route, not the endocrine function of the testis, has been interrupted.

**Conclude.** After vasectomy, sperm are produced and matured but can no longer leave the tract, while testosterone levels remain normal because Leydig cells under LH control continue to secrete androgen independently of the vas deferens.

questions.q: A student in Keren claims that because the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands release a clear fluid before ejaculation, that fluid must be the main carrier of sperm. Explain, using the unit's description of the male accessory glands, why this claim is incorrect, and state the two functions the bulbourethral glands actually perform.
questions.answer: The claim is incorrect because the bulbourethral glands contribute only a small clear, viscous pre-ejaculatory mucus; the bulk of semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles (about 60%) and the prostate gland (about 30%). Their two functions are lubricating the urethra and neutralizing residual acidic urine prior to ejaculation.
why: **Establish the actual volume contributions.** The unit states that the seminal vesicles contribute approximately $$60\%$$ of total semen volume and the prostate gland about $$30\%$$. Together these two glands account for about $$90\%$$ of semen, leaving only roughly $$10\%$$ for the bulbourethral gland secretion and the spermatozoa themselves.

**Show why the student's claim fails.** A secretion that forms only a small fraction of the ejaculate cannot be its main carrier of sperm. The spermatozoa themselves are the cellular component, suspended in the fluid vehicle formed mainly by the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.

**State the real functions of the bulbourethral glands.** The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands secrete a clear, viscous, pre-ejaculatory mucus whose functions are to lubricate the urethra and to neutralize residual acidic urine before semen passes. These are preparatory and protective roles, not a sperm-carrying role.

**Conclude.** The claim is incorrect: the bulbourethral secretion is a minor pre-ejaculatory lubricating and neutralizing fluid, while the seminal vesicles and prostate gland provide the bulk of the semen volume.

options.B: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, so Leydig cell stimulation falls and testosterone production is reduced.
options.C: Testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion but on the anterior pituitary to increase LH release, so the two effects cancel and testosterone production is unchanged.
options.D: Testosterone acts directly on the seminiferous tubules to decrease spermatogenesis, and the reduced sperm numbers feed back on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release.

why: **Identify the axis being regulated.** Testosterone secretion is governed by the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) axis: the hypothalamus releases Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), which drives the anterior pituitary to release LH, and LH stimulates the Leydig cells of the testis to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

**State the direction of a negative feedback loop.** In negative feedback, a rise in the level of the final hormone in the chain suppresses the earlier steps of the chain. The unit states explicitly that as blood testosterone levels rise, testosterone acts on the hypothalamus to decrease GnRH secretion and on the anterior pituitary to decrease LH release, stabilizing hormone levels.

**Evaluate each option.** Option A describes positive feedback, in which rising testosterone would further increase GnRH and LH, which contradicts the stabilizing negative feedback the unit describes; it also misstates the effect on both organs. Option C is internally inconsistent, since the unit gives decreases at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. Option D introduces a sperm-count feedback signal that the unit never describes, and the unit's loop is defined by blood testosterone acting on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, not on the seminiferous tubules.

**Confirm the correct option and its consequence.** Option B matches the unit exactly: decreased GnRH and decreased LH. With less LH reaching the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells are less stimulated, testosterone secretion falls, and the elevated blood level is brought back down toward its stable value.
**Conclude.** Rising blood testosterone suppresses the HPG axis at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, so option B is the correct statement of the feedback response.

questions.q: A laboratory report for a patient in Asmara shows a very low blood testosterone level together with an abnormally high LH level, and the hypothalamic GnRH secretion is found to be high. Which single structure does this pattern indicate is failing, and what is the normal response of that structure to LH?
questions.answer: The Leydig cells (interstitial cells) of the testis are failing. Normally LH from the anterior pituitary stimulates the Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, so unrepaired Leydig cells should raise testosterone output when LH is high.
why: **Read the pattern of hormones.** GnRH is high and LH is high, so the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary are both sending strong stimulatory signals down the HPG axis. The defect therefore lies below the pituitary.

**Identify the target of LH.** The unit states that the Leydig cells, the interstitial cells lying between adjacent seminiferous tubules, synthesize and secrete androgens, primarily testosterone, when stimulated by Luteinizing Hormone secreted from the anterior pituitary.

**Explain why high LH with low testosterone is diagnostic.** If the Leydig cells were responding normally, a high LH level would drive testosterone production upward. Instead testosterone remains very low, so the Leydig cells are not responding to LH stimulation and are the failing structure.

**Account for the high upstream hormones.** Because testosterone is the signal that suppresses the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary, low testosterone removes that inhibition. GnRH and LH therefore remain high, which is exactly what the report shows.
**Conclude.** The failing structure is the Leydig cell population of the testis, whose normal response to LH is to synthesize and secrete testosterone.

questions.q: A man in Keren receives a treatment that keeps his blood testosterone concentration artificially high for several weeks. Predict the effect of this treatment on the secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone and Luteinizing Hormone, and explain how the treatment will affect the activity of his Leydig cells.
questions.answer: GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus and LH release from the anterior pituitary will both decrease through negative feedback; with less LH stimulation the Leydig cells will become less active and their own testosterone secretion will fall.
why: **Recognise the feedback signal.** Blood testosterone is the final hormone of the HPG axis and acts as the inhibitory signal on the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary. An artificially raised level therefore acts as a strong inhibitory signal.
**Predict the hypothalamic response.** The hypothalamus responds by decreasing its secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone, the hormone that normally drives the anterior pituitary.
**Predict the pituitary response.** The anterior pituitary responds to the raised testosterone directly, as well as to the reduced GnRH, by decreasing its release of Luteinizing Hormone.

**Trace the effect on Leydig cells.** Leydig cells synthesize and secrete testosterone when stimulated by LH. With LH release suppressed, the Leydig cells receive less stimulation and become less active, so the testis's own contribution to blood testosterone declines even while the external treatment maintains a high total level.
**Conclude.** Sustained high blood testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH through negative feedback, and the reduced LH stimulation in turn lowers the secretory activity of the Leydig cells.

questions.q: State two reasons why the testes are found in the scrotum.
questions.answer: Sperm production needs a temperature 3–5 °C below body temperature, which the scrotum provides; the scrotal muscles can also adjust the testes’ position (and so temperature) — relaxing to cool them and contracting to warm them.
why: Step 1: temperature requirement.
Step 2: regulation by the scrotal muscles.
questions.tip: Always link scrotum → temperature → sperm.

similar.q: What may tight underwear do to fertility? Why?
similar.a: Reduce it, by holding the testes against the warm body.

why: Step 1: the developing testes secrete testosterone.
Step 2: testosterone stimulates their descent (textbook p.28).
questions.tip: The testes move themselves using their own hormone.

similar.q: What is the condition called when the testes do not descend?
similar.a: Undescended testes (cryptorchidism) — causes infertility.

questions.label: 2.2 Practice — male reproductive system

questions.q: Describe how spermatogenesis takes place.
questions.answer: It begins at puberty in the seminiferous tubules. Spermatogonia (formed in fetal life) divide by mitosis; some grow into spermatocytes, which divide by meiosis to form haploid spermatids; these develop a head with acrosome, a middle piece with mitochondria and a tail, becoming sperm, which are matured in the epididymis.
why: Step 1: where and when.
Step 2: mitosis → spermatocytes.
Step 3: meiosis → spermatids (23 chromosomes).
Step 4: shape change → sperm.
Step 5: maturation in the epididymis.
questions.tip: Use the order: gonia → cytes → tids → zoa.

similar.q: Why must meiosis happen in sperm formation?
similar.a: To halve the chromosome number so the zygote has 46, not 92.

questions.q: Semen consists of

options.B: sperm and secretions of the accessory glands

why: Step 1: sperm come from the testes.
Step 2: seminal vesicles, prostate and Cowper’s glands add fluid.
Step 3: together = semen.
questions.tip: Semen = sperm + seminal fluid.

similar.q: Name two substances in semen besides sperm.
similar.a: Sugar (food), enzymes, alkaline fluid, prostaglandins, mucus.

questions.q: Circumcision is described as hygienic. Explain.
questions.answer: Circumcision removes the foreskin. Without the foreskin, secretions and dirt cannot collect under it, so there is less risk of odour and bacterial infection. An uncircumcised man must clean under the foreskin daily.
why: Step 1: define circumcision.
Step 2: what collects under the foreskin.
Step 3: consequence for infection.
questions.tip: Define first, then give the reason.

similar.q: What tissue in the penis fills with blood during an erection?
similar.a: Spongy (erectile) tissue.

Step 2: they cause contractions in the female organs that help sperm move to the ovum.
questions.tip: Prostaglandins = “push” chemicals.

similar.q: What is the main role of Cowper’s gland mucus?
similar.a: Lubrication.

questions.q: Arrange in order the structures through which sperm pass from where they are made to the outside.
questions.answer: Seminiferous tubules (testis) → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra (in the penis) → outside.
why: Step 1: made in the tubules.
Step 2: stored in the epididymis.
Step 3: carried by the vas deferens.
Step 4: leave through the urethra.
questions.tip: Use the mnemonic SEVEN UP.

similar.q: At which point do the seminal vesicle secretions join?
similar.a: Where the vas deferens joins the urethra (ejaculatory duct).

similar.q: What happens in the epididymis?
similar.a: Sperm are stored temporarily and mature.

questions.q: Describe the roles of FSH and LH in the female.
questions.answer: FSH stimulates the growth of follicles in the ovary and the production of oestrogen by follicle cells. LH (its mid-cycle surge) causes ovulation and makes the corpus luteum secrete progesterone.
why: Step 1: FSH → follicle + oestrogen.
Step 2: LH → ovulation.
Step 3: LH → corpus luteum → progesterone.
questions.tip: F = Follicle; L = Luteum.

similar.q: Give the roles of FSH and LH in males.
similar.a: FSH: sperm formation in the tubules; LH: testosterone from interstitial cells.

questions.q: Identical twins are formed when

options.A: two ova are fertilized by two sperm
options.B: one zygote divides into two separate embryos
options.C: one ovum is fertilized by two sperm
options.D: a zygote divides but fails to separate

why: Step 1: identical = same genes = one zygote.
Step 2: the zygote splits into two embryos that separate fully.
Step 3: option D describes Siamese twins.
questions.tip: One egg → identical; two eggs → fraternal.

similar.q: Can fraternal twins be a boy and a girl?
similar.a: Yes — they come from two different eggs and sperm.

questions.label: 2.3 Practice — female reproductive system

questions.q: Explain why menstruation stops during pregnancy.
questions.answer: The corpus luteum and then the placenta keep secreting progesterone (and oestrogen). Progesterone maintains the uterine lining and stops new follicles developing, so there is no ovulation and the lining is not shed.
why: Step 1: menstruation needs progesterone to fall.
Step 2: in pregnancy progesterone stays high.
Step 3: lining kept; ovulation stopped.
questions.tip: Link the event to the hormone level.

similar.q: Which organ takes over hormone secretion from the corpus luteum?
similar.a: The placenta.

similar.q: Name one harmful substance that can cross the placenta.

questions.q: Describe the main events of childbirth.
questions.answer: Regular powerful contractions of the uterus begin (labour), strengthened by oxytocin; the amnion bursts and the fluid lubricates the birth canal; the cervix and vagina dilate; the baby is pushed out head first; the cord is cut; the placenta and remaining cord are expelled as the afterbirth; the cord stump falls off, leaving the navel.

Step 2: waters break.
Step 3: dilation.
Step 4: delivery head first.
Step 5: afterbirth.
Step 6: navel forms.
questions.tip: Write the events in time order with one key word each.

similar.a: The scar left where the umbilical cord stump fell off.

questions.q: State the function of each: (a) fimbriae (b) cervix (c) endometrium.
questions.answer: (a) Fimbriae sweep the released ovum into the fallopian tube. (b) The cervix closes the uterus during pregnancy and dilates during birth. (c) The endometrium thickens to receive and nourish the embryo; it is shed in menstruation.

Step 2: cervix → close/open.
Step 3: endometrium → bed for the embryo.
questions.tip: One verb per structure: catch, close, cushion.

similar.q: What is the function of cilia in the oviduct?
similar.a: To move the ovum (or zygote) towards the uterus.
